title: Lunar influence and the illusion of scale
english: Twelve times the year completes its course, being a poetic one, except that it requires an intercalary month for the exactness of the hours. For the solar year is a restoration from the same point to the same point according to the sun's own motion. When the moon wanes, the bodies of animals are thinned and become hollow; but when it waxes, they are replenished. This is because it secretly pours in moisture along with heat; for those sleeping under the moon are filled in the heads with excessive moisture, and the fresh-eating of meats, and whatever is of this kind, is quickly turned by the impact of the moon. Similarly, the things concerning the air arise from such a cause. For when a new moon is present and the calm is steady, sudden wind disturbances occur, with clouds being shaken and falling upon one another; and there are torrents around the fair-winded places, and a surging of the sea around the ocean. If even a solar eclipse occurs when there is a new moon, it happens more violently; for the moon, having passed below, obstructs the rays of the sun. Great indeed this moon has become.

But idle myths were preserved everywhere by drunken sailors: that it is moved from its own seat by certain levers and is carried toward the earth. And what kind of place would have received it after it had landed? For the appearance of it being something small did not deceive. For our vision, becoming small, made the things seen also seem small, bringing the natural passion upon visible things. For just as if someone were to view fields and oxen grazing at once from a distance, he would not seem to see an ant's fantasy; for the vision, having been obscured by the air and having become unsteady, is not sufficient for the exact understanding of the things seen. And that the body of the moon is immense, it is possible to learn from evidences. For all the cities throughout the inhabited world, most widely separated from one another, having been divided into four parts toward the east, equally receive the lunar light, and likewise those dwelling in the west, and the midday and northern parts, observe it.

And on the fifth day God commanded the waters to bring forth living souls according to their kind; and immediately the sea produced diverse kinds of all animals. Of the waves, some are amphibians, such as seals, and crocodiles, and the river horses, and also frogs, and crabs, but they do not have the swimming ability; for they are creeping by nature, being drawn toward the head of the water; but the live-bearing ones are seals, and dolphins, and rays, and those similar to them.

But God commanded also to prefer the deep ones, the coastal ones, the bottom ones, the rocky ones, the herd-like ones, the sporadic ones, the sea-monsters, the huge ones, and the very smallest of the fishes, having a natural kinship to the water. For if they are separated from the water a little, not having breath, they are destroyed; for the expansion and the covering of the gills, receiving the water and passing it through, possesses this breath. They do not have teeth halfway, but all their teeth are densely packed and sharp, so that by not being worn down by time, they may chew the food. For it was meant to be destroyed by the water in fine chewing. And nothing else emits a scent from them except the scabbard-fish.

And there is also other food suitable for others. For some are fed on mud, others on seaweeds, others on grasses nourished by the water; others are cannibals. And there are also diverse characteristics among them. The sawfish has long fins; and having seen a ship sailing straight, it, having raised its own fins, imitates the shapes of the ship's movement, and swims with those sailing. Having thus made forty stadia and having labored, it lowers its fins and is carried by the waves to its own place.

The sea-monster is called Aspidochelone by some; and it is by nature most immense, so as often to instill in those sailing the fantasy of a great island. For when it rises from the depths, its body appears like rough stones, and those plunging poles around it release the boats, which immediately sink, the sea-monster having been warmed by the sun and having dived into the depths. It also has a heavy voice by nature, and when hungry, opens its mouth and sends out a most fragrant exhalation, so as to lure the small fishes and to press them all into its mouth. title: Nature of Sea and River Creatures
english: The Atlantic seas are great in size. As for the crab, the flesh of the oyster is edible; but since it is unable to open the folding of its shells, it watches for the folds to be opened in remote places, and being delighted by the sunlight, it takes a pebble and inserts it secretly, then closes the folding, and thus easily destroys it. The sea urchin foreknows the onset of winter, and carries a pebble so as not to be tossed about by the force of the waves. The octopus, having rushed against a certain rock, became of the same color as it, and it destroys the fish approaching the rock.

The nautilus is the smallest in nature, yet it stands up being carried by a gale as if the greatest of ships, so that the ship seems to be lost in the sea. In the river there is the hydra, having the form of a dog, which is an enemy to the crocodile and destroys him while he sleeps. For the crocodile sleeps having opened its own mouth; and the hydra, having curled itself into the mud [ph. having coiled itself], leaps into its mouth, and by destroying everything inside it, it destroys him.

The crocodile is a beast both like a land animal and a fish, great from head to tail, though it does not have a width in proportion to its size. Its back is thin like a stream, the color of its back is like black stone, and its belly is white. Its feet are four, curved toward the side, much like the land turtle; it has a long and thick tail, for it is the end of a single spine. It is notched from above into spines, which are like the teeth of saws, and it strikes with them against those whom it might beat. One of its heads is joined to the backs, standing straight in a single measure; as far as it has not opened, it is a beast's head, but if it loses this, it becomes a whole mouth, making a chasm even unto the shoulders.

The so-called hippopotamus has the feet and the belly of a horse, and its weapon is split like a hoof, with a thick tail that is thin of hair, because the whole of its body is thus: a head that is circular, slightly different from the cheek of a horse, and it has a hollowed nose breathing a fiery smoke, as from a furnace, having a wide snout; for it opens the mouth even unto the temples.

Its interior is densely hairy, possessing two curved teeth like a boar. The whole thing is very easy to swallow, making it food. It is hunted in this way: the hunters watch it, dig a pit, cover it with a reed, sprinkle it with sand, and build a wooden house below, having the doors open toward the roof of the pit; when the beast climbs upon it, it falls helplessly, and is trapped inside the house being carried down. Then the hunters immediately close it. Second... the small beast makes a loud noise.

In the fish, there is much internal heat and sharpness; therefore they fall [prey] more easily, eating things that immediately tear the edible parts within their bellies. The sea-fox, if it is unable to escape the net, swallowing the bait, leaping and running, drives away the sea-urchin and flees. The crocodile is a man-eating beast; when it is about to make its nests, having surveyed, it turns the female onto the banks; for this alone is accustomed to approach lying on its back, and after the interaction, striking her again with its hands, it turns her back; when it perceives her to be related to another, it pretends to mingle with her, and in the same way, having turned her, it recognizes her by the smell (for it has a sharp sense for this) having been impregnated by another, and having torn her belly with its claws, it eats everything within it. For the animal is tender around the belly; for its back is clothed in hard scales, so that even the sharpest iron, when brought against it, is blunted.

Let the winged creatures bring forth living souls from the waters, and suddenly the air is filled with all kinds of birds. He gave them their origin from the waters, since they have been allotted a certain kinship to the fish. Just as the fish cut the water with the movement of their fins and move through it, so the winged ones move through the air with their wings. Among them, the carnivores possess a construction appropriate to their slaughtering diet, having sharp claws, a curved lip, and a sharp wing to easily snatch and tear apart; but the seed-eaters and those fed on everything [are different]. title: Nature's varied dispositions
english: They are diverse; for some are lawless and autonomous, while others are ordered under a ruler, some are migratory, and others are local. The peacock is the one that crows, but the hawk is most favorable regarding man.

For it is reported that in Thrace the hawks are joined to the bird-hunters regarding the hunt; for they spend their time in thick woods, where a kind of birds dwells, and they coordinate with those going to the hunt to receive a share of what is caught. And when the hunters shake the trees, the birds, being startled, cry out and fly up, and the hawks, swooping down over their heads, strike their heads and cast them to the ground, preparing an easy hunt for men; and those who are without the hunt immediately receive a share of it.

The pelican is a lover of its young; for while feeding the chicks, they strike him in the face with their wings; but he who strikes them destroys them, and being moved to pity, he mourns them for three days. And the mother, coming upon them, tears her side, and her blood drips upon the chicks, and they are brought to life. These pelicans eat the shells in this way: being unable to release them because they are gripped, they swallow them first, so that by the heat around the pharynx, the adhering glue may be loosened and the shells may be softened; having dissolved them, they easily eat their food. And the nests are not where they hatch, but, because of the multitude of hunters, they move to another place to rear the young. And when they perceive some of the young ones having arrived for the hunt, they fly up and divert the haste of the hunters toward themselves, providing a time of flight for the young; and after the young have escaped, they carry themselves very boldly with the young, as if walking on the air.

The peacock is a lover of beauty, rushing from India. This one, having spread his beauty and shown the spectacle of his wings, is led toward a meeting with the female, just as a peacock shows this adornment to her; for the peacock is almost like a beautiful garden.

For gold is planted around its wings, and a circular woven pattern surrounds the purple gold; and an equal circle is enclosed by the gold, and there is an eye in a wing. The phoenix has the size of a peacock, but differs from the peacock in color; for its wings have been dyed with gold and purple, and its head is naturally adorned in the shape of a circular crown. And the circle is azure, and rose-like. Being well-formed in appearance, and adorned with rays, as if a sun stands on high; as others have recorded the form of this body, as they themselves describe it thus: for its length is almost double that of an eagle. With various wings and colors, its body is burned. Its breast, indeed, appears purple, but its legs are millet-colored, and at the neck, it is elegantly arranged with saffron-colored hairs. And its head is like a bed of days, and it looked toward the girl with a millet-grain. And it appeared like a grain of millet to the girls. And it had a voice most pleasant to all. And it appeared as king of all birds, as one might perceive; for all birds, wandering long away behind it, fell down. And itself, like a bull boasting, was walking with a firm step, bearing the weight of its foot.

They say this exists as a unique animal, not existing by succession, but existing most alone, and living five hundred years. And at the time when it is about to perish (for it foresees its own death), having aimed for some high place, at the rising of the sun, it gathers its beauty from aromatic twigs, and then is consumed by the ray of the sun, and is completely dissolved into dust; then from the dust worms are produced, and from the worm into the first phoenix it is transformed.

But the eagle is most unjust regarding the nourishment of the young; for having done two things, it makes one inhabit with it, and it sends the other away by chewing it with its wings, through the food, as they say, the venom. But the phoenix, having received the one left behind, simultaneously nourishes the young ones with the inhabitants. And having nourished the young one, the eagle falls upon it, taking it toward the ether; and if it were to see it having sharpened itself against the brightness of the sun, and boldly resounding through the air, it makes it its own inhabitant; but if it is unformed toward these things, it casts it off as a bastard.
